items.stem: Which part of an alkene is attacked by electrophiles?
items.answer: the π bond of C=C
items.markingKey: A. Electron-rich region above and below the plane.

items.stem: Why is the product of adding Br₂ to ethene saturated?
options: The π bond is broken and every carbon forms four single bonds.
items.answer: The π bond is broken and every carbon forms four single bonds.
items.markingKey: C. Addition removes unsaturation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the major product and the minor product of HBr addition to propene.
items.answer: The major product (2-bromopropane) forms via the more stable secondary carbocation; the minor product (1-bromopropane) forms via the less stable primary carbocation.
items.markingKey: The major product (2-bromopropane) forms via the more stable secondary carbocation; the minor product (1-bromopropane) forms via the less stable primary carbocation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: But-1-ene reacts with HCl. Name the major and minor organic products and explain which is major.
items.answer: major: 2-chlorobutane; minor: 1-chlorobutane. The major product forms via the more stable secondary carbocation (CH₃CH₂CH⁺CH₃), stabilised by the positive inductive effect of its alkyl groups.
items.markingKey: 2-chlorobutane major (1); 1-chlorobutane minor (1); secondary carbocation more stable / more alkyl groups donating (1).

items.stem: Which alkene from 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, 2-methylbut-1-ene, but-2-ene and ethene gives a mixture of two structural isomers on reaction with HCl?
items.answer: 2-methylbut-1-ene
items.markingKey: B. 2-methylbut-1-ene is unsymmetrical, so Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov products form.

items.stem: A sample of 0.773 g of an unsaturated hydrocarbon C₁₀H₁₆ decolourised exactly 170 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ bromine solution. Deduce the number of C=C double bonds in one molecule.

Propene reacts with hydrogen bromide. (a) State the type of reaction. (b) Draw the mechanism leading to the major product. (c) Explain why this product is major. (d) Suggest how the ratio of products could be measured.
items.answer: (a) electrophilic addition. (b) curly arrows from π bond to H, from H–Br to Br; CH₃CH⁺CH₃; Br⁻ attacks C⁺ → 2-bromopropane. (c) secondary carbocation more stable than primary (two alkyl groups, positive inductive effect) → forms faster. (d) gas chromatography or ¹H NMR peak ratios of the mixture.
items.markingKey: (a) electrophilic addition. (b) curly arrows from π bond to H, from H–Br to Br; CH₃CH⁺CH₃; Br⁻ attacks C⁺ → 2-bromopropane. (c) secondary carbocation more stable than primary (two alkyl groups, positive inductive effect) → forms faster. (d) gas chromatography or ¹H NMR peak ratios of the mixture.

items.stem:
A student bubbled excess HBr through a solution containing 3.50 g of 2-methylpropene at room temperature. 5.30 g of a liquid product mixture was obtained. Gas chromatography showed two peaks:

compound | peak area / %
2-bromo-2-methylpropane | 94
1-bromo-2-methylpropane | 6

(a) Calculate the percentage yield of the product mixture. [3]
(b) Explain the ratio of products in terms of the mechanism. [2]
(c) Calculate the mass of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane in the mixture. [1]
(d) State why the two products have identical molecular formulas. [1]
(e) Suggest why the reaction is carried out in the dark. [1]
items.answer: (a) 62 % (b) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is major because it forms via the more stable tertiary carbocation; 1-bromo-2-methylpropane forms via a less stable carbocation. (c) 4.98 g (d) They are structural (positional) isomers. (e) To prevent radical substitution side reactions initiated by UV light.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] n(alkene) = 3.50/56.12 = 0.0624 mol (M1); theoretical = 8.55 g (M1); yield = 62 % (A1). (b) [2] carbocation intermediate (1); more alkyl groups / positive inductive effect → more stable (1). (c) [1] 5.30 × 94/100 = 4.98 g (A1), assuming peak area ∝ mass. (d) [1] structural isomers (1). (e) [1] radical reactions avoided (1).

items.stem: Which reagent and condition convert ethene to ethanol industrially?
items.answer: steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst
items.markingKey: B. Hydration.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "electrophilic addition".
items.answer: A reaction in which an electrophile attacks the electron-rich C=C double bond and two species add across it, forming a saturated product
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a reaction in which an electrophile attacks the electron-rich C=C double bond and two species add across it, forming a saturated product. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "positive inductive effect"?
options: A Lewis acid such as FeBr₃ or AlCl₃ that accepts a lone pair from a halogen molecule, polarising it to generate the X⁺ electrophile
A reaction in which an electrophile attacks the electron-rich C=C double bond and two species add across it, forming a saturated product
The donation of electron density through σ bonds by alkyl groups, which stabilises an adjacent positive charge
The positively charged intermediate formed when an electrophile bonds to one ring carbon, temporarily breaking the delocalised system
items.answer: The donation of electron density through σ bonds by alkyl groups, which stabilises an adjacent positive charge
items.markingKey: C. "positive inductive effect" is the donation of electron density through σ bonds by alkyl groups, which stabilises an adjacent positive charge.

items.stem: "Markovnikov's rule says the bromine adds to the carbon with more hydrogen atoms." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens; bromine ends up on the more substituted carbon.
items.markingKey: The hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens; bromine ends up on the more substituted carbon. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of carbocation stability, why propene forms more 2-bromopropane than 1-bromopropane with HBr.
items.answer: Addition of H⁺ to the terminal carbon gives a secondary carbocation, which is stabilised by two alkyl groups (positive inductive effect); it forms faster than the primary carbocation, so its product, 2-bromopropane, is major.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Addition of H⁺ to the terminal carbon gives a secondary carbocation, which is stabilised by two alkyl groups (positive inductive effect); it forms faster than the primary carbocation, so its product, 2-bromopropane, is major. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why is a tertiary carbocation more stable than a secondary one?
options: More alkyl groups push electron density towards the positive carbon.
items.answer: More alkyl groups push electron density towards the positive carbon.
items.markingKey: A. Positive inductive effect.

items.stem: Briefly explain why alkenes undergo addition rather than substitution reactions.
items.answer: The π bond is weaker than the σ bond and its electrons are exposed above and below the plane, so electrophiles attack it; breaking only the π bond and forming two new σ bonds is energetically favourable.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The π bond is weaker than the σ bond and its electrons are exposed above and below the plane, so electrophiles attack it; breaking only the π bond and forming two new σ bonds is energetically favourable. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a primary carbocation and a tertiary carbocation.
items.answer: A primary carbocation has one alkyl group on the positive carbon and is least stable; a tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups donating electron density and is most stable.
items.markingKey: A primary carbocation has one alkyl group on the positive carbon and is least stable; a tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups donating electron density and is most stable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: What is the major organic product when 2-methylbut-2-ene reacts with hydrogen (H₂) under suitable conditions?
items.answer: 2-methylbutane
items.markingKey: D. H₂ adds across the C=C bond to give 2-methylbutane.

items.stem: In the reaction of 2-methylbut-2-ene with HBr, which type of carbocation intermediate leads to the major product, 2-bromo-2-methylbutane?
items.answer: tertiary
items.markingKey: C. (CH₃)₂C⁺CH₂CH₃ is tertiary; the more substituted carbocation is more stable.

items.stem: 0.282 g of a hydrocarbon C₆H₁₀ reacted completely with 156 cm³ of hydrogen at STP in the presence of a nickel catalyst. Deduce the number of C=C double bonds in one molecule (molar volume = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹).
items.markingKey: A. n(hydrocarbon) = 0.00343 mol (M1); n(H₂) = 156/22700 = 0.00686 mol (M1); ratio = 2 (A1).

items.stem: 5.55 g of but-1-ene reacted with excess bromine and 12.4 g of 1,2-dibromobutane was isolated. Calculate the percentage yield.
6.77 g of ethene reacted with excess steam (with an acid catalyst) and 9.67 g of ethanol was isolated. Calculate the percentage yield.
Draw the mechanism for the reaction of propene with hydrogen bromide to form the major product.
items.answer: Arrow from C=C to H of HBr; arrow from H–Br bond to Br; secondary carbocation CH₃CH⁺CH₃ and Br⁻; arrow from Br⁻ lone pair to C⁺; product 2-bromopropane.
items.markingKey: Arrow from C=C to H of HBr; arrow from H–Br bond to Br; secondary carbocation CH₃CH⁺CH₃ and Br⁻; arrow from Br⁻ lone pair to C⁺; product 2-bromopropane.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Bromine water is a definitive test for an alkene."
items.answer: It is a good test for C=C unsaturation, but confirmation needs further evidence such as IR or ¹H NMR.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rapid decolourisation at room temperature in the dark; simple and cheap. Arguments against: other unsaturated compounds (alkynes) also decolourise it; phenols and some other compounds react with bromine water; it does not identify which alkene is present. Supported judgement: It is a good test for C=C unsaturation, but confirmation needs further evidence such as IR or ¹H NMR.

(b) Explain the ratio of products in terms of the mechanism. [2]

(d) State why the two products have identical molecular formulas. [1]
(e) Suggest why the reaction is carried out in the dark. [1]
items.answer: (a) 77 % (b) 2-chlorobutane is major because it forms via the more stable secondary carbocation; 1-chlorobutane forms via a less stable carbocation. (c) 6.08 g (d) They are structural (positional) isomers. (e) To prevent radical substitution side reactions initiated by UV light.

items.stem: Define the term "electrophilic substitution".
items.answer: A reaction in which an electrophile replaces a hydrogen atom on an aromatic ring, so the delocalised π system is retained
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a reaction in which an electrophile replaces a hydrogen atom on an aromatic ring, so the delocalised π system is retained. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition reactions.
items.answer: Addition would permanently destroy the delocalised π system and its stabilisation energy; substitution restores the delocalised ring, so it is energetically favoured.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Addition would permanently destroy the delocalised π system and its stabilisation energy; substitution restores the delocalised ring, so it is energetically favoured. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Benzene has three double bonds and so reacts like an alkene." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Benzene has a delocalised π system; it does not behave as three isolated C=C bonds and prefers substitution.
items.markingKey: Benzene has a delocalised π system; it does not behave as three isolated C=C bonds and prefers substitution. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Benzene is treated with chlorine with an aluminium chloride (or FeCl₃) halogen carrier. What is the electrophile?
items.answer: Cl⁺
items.markingKey: B. Cl₂ + AlCl₃ → Cl⁺ + AlCl₄⁻; electrophile Cl⁺ substitutes one H to give chlorobenzene.

items.stem:
Ana collected the enthalpy changes of hydrogenation of some cyclic hydrocarbons, each forming cyclohexane, from a database.

compound | ΔH / kJ mol⁻¹
benzene | −209
cyclohexene | −119
cyclohexa-1,4-diene | −242
cyclohexa-1,3-diene | −230

(a) Predict the enthalpy of hydrogenation of a hypothetical Kekulé structure, cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. [1]
(b) Calculate the stabilisation energy of benzene. [2]
(c) State the catalyst and one condition used for hydrogenation. [2]
(d) Compare the value for cyclohexa-1,3-diene with 2 × the value for cyclohexene and suggest a reason for the difference. [2]
(e) State one piece of structural evidence for delocalisation in benzene. [1]
items.answer: (a) −357 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) 148 kJ mol⁻¹ (c) nickel, about 150 °C (or Pt/Pd at room temperature) (d) −230 vs −238: slightly less exothermic because the conjugated double bonds have a small amount of delocalisation. (e) All C–C bonds are the same length (140 pm) by X-ray diffraction.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 3 × (−119) (A1). (b) [2] −209 − (−357) = 148 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1); benzene more stable (1). (c) [2] catalyst (1); condition (1). (d) [2] comparison (1); conjugation/partial delocalisation (1). (e) [1] equal bond lengths (1).

items.stem: ΔH(hydrogenation) values: cyclohexene −122 kJ mol⁻¹, cyclohexa-1,3-diene −233 kJ mol⁻¹, benzene −210 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the stabilisation energy of benzene using cyclohexene as the reference. (b) Estimate it again by treating benzene as cyclohexa-1,3-diene plus one further isolated C=C bond. (c) Evaluate which estimate is more reliable and what both show about the Kekulé model.
items.answer: (a) 3 × (−122) = −366; −210 − (−366) = 156 → 156 kJ mol⁻¹. (b) (−233) + (−122) = −355; −210 − (−355) = 145 → 145 kJ mol⁻¹. (c) The second estimate allows for the small conjugation energy of adjacent C=C bonds, so it is closer to a true “localised triene”; both show that benzene is substantially more stable than any Kekulé structure, so the delocalised model is supported.
items.markingKey: (a) 156 (2). (b) 145 (2). (c) judgement on the reference compound (1); conclusion: Kekulé model inadequate / delocalisation (1).

items.stem: What is the shape of the benzene molecule?
items.answer: planar hexagonal
items.markingKey: D. All sp² carbons.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "arenium ion (Wheland intermediate)"?
options: The difference between the enthalpy change expected for a hypothetical Kekulé structure and the actual value, showing the extra stability of the delocalised ring
The positively charged intermediate formed when an electrophile bonds to one ring carbon, temporarily breaking the delocalised system
A reaction in which an electrophile attacks the electron-rich C=C double bond and two species add across it, forming a saturated product
A reaction in which an electrophile replaces a hydrogen atom on an aromatic ring, so the delocalised π system is retained
items.answer: The positively charged intermediate formed when an electrophile bonds to one ring carbon, temporarily breaking the delocalised system
items.markingKey: B. "arenium ion (Wheland intermediate)" is the positively charged intermediate formed when an electrophile bonds to one ring carbon, temporarily breaking the delocalised system.

items.stem: Which evidence best supports the delocalised structure of benzene?
options: It burns with a smoky flame.
Its enthalpy of hydrogenation is less exothermic than 3 × that of cyclohexene.
items.answer: Its enthalpy of hydrogenation is less exothermic than 3 × that of cyclohexene.
items.markingKey: D. About 150 kJ mol⁻¹ extra stability.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the delocalised model of benzene and the Kekulé structure of benzene.
items.answer: The Kekulé structure has alternating single and double bonds of different lengths; the delocalised model has six equal bonds (140 pm) with π electrons spread round the ring.
items.markingKey: The Kekulé structure has alternating single and double bonds of different lengths; the delocalised model has six equal bonds (140 pm) with π electrons spread round the ring. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why does the arenium ion lose H⁺ rather than add a nucleophile?
options: Losing H⁺ restores the stable delocalised ring.
items.answer: Losing H⁺ restores the stable delocalised ring.
items.markingKey: C. Re-aromatisation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the delocalised model of benzene and the Kekulé structure of benzene.
items.answer: The Kekulé structure has alternating single and double bonds of different lengths; the delocalised model has six equal bonds (140 pm) with π electrons spread round the ring.
items.markingKey: The Kekulé structure has alternating single and double bonds of different lengths; the delocalised model has six equal bonds (140 pm) with π electrons spread round the ring. items.stem: The C–C single bond length is 153 pm and the C=C double bond length is 134 pm. Which statement about the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene is consistent with the delocalised model?
options: Three are 153 pm and three are 134 pm.
All six are equal, at about 140 pm.
items.answer: All six are equal, at about 140 pm.
items.markingKey: B. Intermediate bond order of 1.5.

items.stem: 8.67 g of benzene undergoes bromination with bromine with an iron(III) bromide (or AlBr₃) halogen carrier. Calculate the mass of bromobenzene obtained if the yield is 55 %.
Draw the mechanism for the bromination of benzene in the presence of FeBr₃.
items.answer: Arrow from delocalised ring to Br⁺; arenium ion with horseshoe ring and + charge, H and Br on sp³ carbon; arrow from C–H bond into ring; bromobenzene + H⁺ (→ HBr, FeBr₃ regenerated).
items.markingKey: Arrow from delocalised ring to Br⁺; arenium ion with horseshoe ring and + charge, H and Br on sp³ carbon; arrow from C–H bond into ring; bromobenzene + H⁺ (→ HBr, FeBr₃ regenerated).

items.stem: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −122 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene is −210 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the stabilisation energy of benzene relative to a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene.
items.answer: 156 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: expected = 3 × (−122) = −366 kJ mol⁻¹ (M1); stabilisation = −210 − (−366) = 156 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1) (benzene is more stable).

items.stem: 6.29 g of benzene undergoes nitration with concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid at below 55 °C. Calculate the mass of nitrobenzene obtained if the yield is 72 %.

Benzene reacts with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids. (a) Write an equation for the formation of the electrophile. (b) Draw the mechanism. (c) Explain why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition. (d) Calculate the mass of nitrobenzene that could be obtained from 7.81 g of benzene at a 75 % yield.
items.answer: (a) HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. (b) arrow ring → NO₂⁺; arenium ion; C–H bond electrons return to ring; H⁺ lost. (c) substitution keeps the delocalised ring (stabilisation ≈150 kJ mol⁻¹). (d) n = 7.81/78.12 = 0.100 mol; 0.100 × 123.12 × 0.75 = 9.23 g.
items.markingKey: (a) HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. (b) arrow ring → NO₂⁺; arenium ion; C–H bond electrons return to ring; H⁺ lost. (c) substitution keeps the delocalised ring (stabilisation ≈150 kJ mol⁻¹). (d) n = 7.81/78.12 = 0.100 mol; 0.100 × 123.12 × 0.75 = 9.23 g.

items.stem: "Using enthalpies of hydrogenation gives an accurate value for the stabilisation energy of benzene." Discuss.
items.answer: It gives a reasonable estimate (about 150 kJ mol⁻¹) but not an exact value, as it depends on the reference compound.

(a) Calculate the stabilisation energy of benzene using cyclohexene as the reference. (b) Estimate it again by treating benzene as cyclohexa-1,3-diene plus one further isolated C=C bond. (c) Evaluate which estimate is more reliable and what both show about the Kekulé model.
items.answer: (a) 3 × (−118) = −354; −208 − (−354) = 146 → 146 kJ mol⁻¹. (b) (−234) + (−118) = −352; −208 − (−352) = 144 → 144 kJ mol⁻¹. (c) The second estimate allows for the small conjugation energy of adjacent C=C bonds, so it is closer to a true “localised triene”; both show that benzene is substantially more stable than any Kekulé structure, so the delocalised model is supported.
items.markingKey: (a) 146 (2). (b) 144 (2). (c) judgement on the reference compound (1); conclusion: Kekulé model inadequate / delocalisation (1).

items.answer: reduction

items.stem: Which reagents and conditions convert a primary alcohol into an aldehyde?

acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil the product as it forms

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Retrosynthesis is the most effective way to plan an organic synthesis."
items.answer: Retrosynthesis is a powerful planning tool, but each proposed step must be evaluated practically.

items.answer: Distillation removes a volatile product as it forms (e.g. an aldehyde); reflux keeps all substances in the flask so reaction goes to completion (e.g. carboxylic acid).

items.stem: Briefly explain why chemists prefer short synthetic routes.
items.answer: Fewer steps give a higher overall yield, use less reagent and energy, produce less waste and save time, improving atom economy and green credentials.

items.stem: Propanoic acid is converted into propanal via propan-1-ol. Which reagents are used, in order?
options: 1: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil the product as it forms; 2: LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then dilute acid
1: LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then dilute acid; 2: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil the product as it forms
1: LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then dilute acid; 2: excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heat under reflux
1: NaBH₄ in water or ethanol; 2: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil the product as it forms
items.answer: 1: LiAlH₄ in dry ether, then dilute acid; 2: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distil the product as it forms
items.markingKey: B. propanoic acid → propan-1-ol (reduction); propan-1-ol → propanal (oxidation).

items.stem: A 4-step synthesis has step yields of 70 %, 79 %, 79 %, 77 %. Calculate the overall percentage yield.

Ethyl ethanoate can be made from ethene in three steps. (a) Outline the route with reagents and conditions. (b) State the type of each reaction. (c) If the step yields are 90 %, 80 % and 65 %, calculate the overall yield. (d) Suggest one way the synthesis could be made greener.
items.answer: (a) ethene + steam/H₃PO₄ → ethanol; some ethanol + excess K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺, reflux → ethanoic acid; ethanol + ethanoic acid, conc. H₂SO₄, heat → ethyl ethanoate. (b) electrophilic addition; oxidation; condensation (esterification). (c) 0.90 × 0.80 × 0.65 = 46.8 %. (d) bio-ethanol from fermentation / recycle unreacted materials / use less hazardous oxidants.
items.markingKey: (a) ethene + steam/H₃PO₄ → ethanol; some ethanol + excess K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺, reflux → ethanoic acid; ethanol + ethanoic acid, conc. H₂SO₄, heat → ethyl ethanoate. (b) electrophilic addition; oxidation; condensation (esterification). (c) 0.90 × 0.80 × 0.65 = 46.8 %. (d) bio-ethanol from fermentation / recycle unreacted materials / use less hazardous oxidants.

items.stem:
Sana collected the enthalpy changes of hydrogenation of some cyclic hydrocarbons, each forming cyclohexane, from a database.

compound | ΔH / kJ mol⁻¹
cyclohexa-1,3-diene | −230
cyclohexene | −120
benzene | −210

(a) Predict the enthalpy of hydrogenation of a hypothetical Kekulé structure, cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. [1]
(b) Calculate the stabilisation energy of benzene. [2]
(c) Compare the value for cyclohexa-1,3-diene with 2 × the value for cyclohexene and suggest a reason for the difference. [2]
(d) State one piece of structural evidence for delocalisation in benzene. [1]
(e) State the catalyst and one condition used for hydrogenation. [2]
items.answer: (a) −360 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) 150 kJ mol⁻¹ (c) −230 vs −240: slightly less exothermic because the conjugated double bonds have a small amount of delocalisation. (d) All C–C bonds are the same length (140 pm) by X-ray diffraction. (e) nickel, about 150 °C (or Pt/Pd at room temperature)
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 3 × (−120) (A1). (b) [2] −210 − (−360) = 150 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1); benzene more stable (1). (c) [2] comparison (1); conjugation/partial delocalisation (1). (d) [1] equal bond lengths (1). (e) [2] catalyst (1); condition (1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The positively charged species formed when the electrophile bonds to one carbon of the C=C bond, leaving the other carbon with only three bonds"?
items.answer: carbocation intermediate
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of carbocation intermediate.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The electrophile NO₂⁺, formed when concentrated sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, which then loses water"?
items.answer: nitronium ion
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of nitronium ion.

items.stem: Which reaction type converts propanone into propan-2-ol?
items.answer: reduction
items.markingKey: reduction. Hydride adds to C=O.

items.stem: A student claims: "Markovnikov's rule says the bromine adds to the carbon with more hydrogen atoms." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens; bromine ends up on the more substituted carbon.
items.markingKey: The hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens; bromine ends up on the more substituted carbon. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why benzene does not decolourise bromine water at room temperature, whereas cyclohexene does.
items.answer: The delocalised electron density in benzene is spread over six atoms and is less concentrated than in a localised C=C bond, so it cannot polarise Br₂ enough without a halogen carrier.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The delocalised electron density in benzene is spread over six atoms and is less concentrated than in a localised C=C bond, so it cannot polarise Br₂ enough without a halogen carrier. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why is NaBH₄ chosen rather than LiAlH₄ to reduce propanone in the laboratory?
options: NaBH₄ is safer and can be used in water or ethanol.
NaBH₄ is a stronger reducing agent.
items.answer: NaBH₄ is safer and can be used in water or ethanol.
items.markingKey: B. LiAlH₄ reacts violently with water.

items.stem: Why does the C=C bond of an alkene attract electrophiles?
options: It is a region of high electron density due to the π bond.
items.answer: It is a region of high electron density due to the π bond.
items.markingKey: A. Exposed π electrons.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the reaction of bromine with cyclohexene and the reaction of bromine with benzene.
items.answer: Cyclohexene undergoes rapid electrophilic addition at room temperature without a catalyst; benzene needs a halogen carrier and undergoes electrophilic substitution, keeping its ring.
items.markingKey: Cyclohexene undergoes rapid electrophilic addition at room temperature without a catalyst; benzene needs a halogen carrier and undergoes electrophilic substitution, keeping its ring. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why is an aldehyde distilled off as it forms during the oxidation of a primary alcohol?
options: To prevent its further oxidation to a carboxylic acid.
items.answer: To prevent its further oxidation to a carboxylic acid.
items.markingKey: B. Aldehyde has the lowest b.p.

items.stem: What is the major organic product when 2-methylpropene reacts with steam (H₂O) under suitable conditions?
items.answer: 2-methylpropan-2-ol
items.markingKey: A. 2-methylpropan-2-ol forms via the tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺.

items.stem: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −118 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene is −211 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the stabilisation energy of benzene relative to a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene.
items.answer: 143 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: C. expected = 3 × (−118) = −354 kJ mol⁻¹ (M1); stabilisation = −211 − (−354) = 143 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1) (benzene is more stable).

items.stem: A 4-step synthesis has step yields of 83 %, 71 %, 78 %, 64 %. Calculate the overall percentage yield.

0.287 g of a hydrocarbon C₄H₆ reacted completely with 241 cm³ of hydrogen at STP in the presence of a nickel catalyst. Deduce the number of C=C double bonds in one molecule (molar volume = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹).
items.markingKey: D. n(hydrocarbon) = 0.00530 mol (M1); n(H₂) = 241/22700 = 0.0106 mol (M1); ratio = 2 (A1).

items.stem: Benzene is treated with bromine with an iron(III) bromide (or AlBr₃) halogen carrier. What is the electrophile?
items.answer: Br⁺
items.markingKey: C. Br₂ + FeBr₃ → Br⁺ + FeBr₄⁻; electrophile Br⁺ substitutes one H to give bromobenzene.

items.stem: Outline a two-step synthesis of phenylamine from benzene.
items.answer: Step 1: conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ below 55 °C → nitrobenzene; Step 2: Sn/conc. HCl, reflux, then NaOH → phenylamine.
items.markingKey: Step 1: conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ below 55 °C → nitrobenzene; Step 2: Sn/conc. HCl, reflux, then NaOH → phenylamine.

items.stem: In the reaction of 2-methylpropene with HI, which type of carbocation intermediate leads to the major product, 2-iodo-2-methylpropane?
items.answer: tertiary
items.markingKey: B. (CH₃)₃C⁺ is tertiary; the more substituted carbocation is more stable.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Kekulé's structure of benzene is an adequate model."
items.answer: It is inadequate: structural and thermochemical evidence supports the delocalised model.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains the formula C₆H₆ and the hexagonal ring; useful for counting electrons in mechanisms. Arguments against: predicts unequal bond lengths – all are 140 pm; predicts addition with bromine water; predicts a hydrogenation enthalpy of −360, not −208 kJ mol⁻¹; predicts two isomers of 1,2-dibromobenzene. Supported judgement: It is inadequate: structural and thermochemical evidence supports the delocalised model.

items.stem:
A student bubbled excess HBr through a solution containing 4.49 g of propene at room temperature. 9.05 g of a liquid product mixture was obtained. Gas chromatography showed two peaks:

compound | peak area / %
2-bromopropane | 80
1-bromopropane | 20

(a) Calculate the percentage yield of the product mixture. [3]
(b) Explain the ratio of products in terms of the mechanism. [2]
(c) Calculate the mass of 2-bromopropane in the mixture. [1]
(d) State why the two products have identical molecular formulas. [1]
(e) Suggest why the reaction is carried out in the dark. [1]
items.answer: (a) 69 % (b) 2-bromopropane is major because it forms via the more stable secondary carbocation; 1-bromopropane forms via a less stable carbocation. (c) 7.24 g (d) They are structural (positional) isomers. (e) To prevent radical substitution side reactions initiated by UV light.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] n(alkene) = 4.49/42.09 = 0.107 mol (M1); theoretical = 13.1 g (M1); yield = 69 % (A1). (b) [2] carbocation intermediate (1); more alkyl groups / positive inductive effect → more stable (1). (c) [1] 9.05 × 80/100 = 7.24 g (A1), assuming peak area ∝ mass. (d) [1] structural isomers (1). (e) [1] radical reactions avoided (1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Bromine water is a definitive test for an alkene."
items.answer: It is a good test for C=C unsaturation, but confirmation needs further evidence such as IR or ¹H NMR.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rapid decolourisation at room temperature in the dark; simple and cheap. Arguments against: other unsaturated compounds (alkynes) also decolourise it; phenols and some other compounds react with bromine water; it does not identify which alkene is present. Supported judgement: It is a good test for C=C unsaturation, but confirmation needs further evidence such as IR or ¹H NMR. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem:
Zara collected the enthalpy changes of hydrogenation of some cyclic hydrocarbons, each forming cyclohexane, from a database.

compound | ΔH / kJ mol⁻¹
cyclohexene | −119
benzene | −210
cyclohexa-1,3-diene | −232

(a) Predict the enthalpy of hydrogenation of a hypothetical Kekulé structure, cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. [1]
(b) Calculate the stabilisation energy of benzene. [2]
(c) State one piece of structural evidence for delocalisation in benzene. [1]
(d) Explain why benzene reacts with bromine by substitution rather than addition. [2]
(e) Compare the value for cyclohexa-1,3-diene with 2 × the value for cyclohexene and suggest a reason for the difference. [2]
items.answer: (a) −357 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) 147 kJ mol⁻¹ (c) All C–C bonds are the same length (140 pm) by X-ray diffraction. (d) Substitution keeps the delocalised ring and its stabilisation energy; addition would destroy it. (e) −232 vs −238: slightly less exothermic because the conjugated double bonds have a small amount of delocalisation.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 3 × (−119) (A1). (b) [2] −210 − (−357) = 147 kJ mol⁻¹ (A1); benzene more stable (1). (c) [1] equal bond lengths (1). (d) [2] delocalisation retained (1); energetically favoured (1). (e) [2] comparison (1); conjugation/partial delocalisation (1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Markovnikov's rule"?
options: When HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogen atoms, so X bonds to the more substituted carbon
A Lewis acid such as FeBr₃ or AlCl₃ that accepts a lone pair from a halogen molecule, polarising it to generate the X⁺ electrophile
The product of the fractional yields of each step in a multi-step synthesis, expressed as a percentage
The temporary polarisation of the Br–Br bond, Brᵟ⁺–Brᵟ⁻, caused by repulsion from the electron-rich π bond of an approaching alkene
items.answer: When HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogen atoms, so X bonds to the more substituted carbon
items.markingKey: A. "Markovnikov's rule" is when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom adds to the carbon that already has more hydrogen atoms, so X bonds to the more substituted carbon.

items.stem: What is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?
items.answer: NO₂⁺
items.markingKey: C. Nitronium ion.

items.stem: Define the term "reaction pathway".
items.answer: A sequence of reactions, each with stated reagents and conditions, that converts a starting material into a target compound
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a sequence of reactions, each with stated reagents and conditions, that converts a starting material into a target compound. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between electrophilic addition to alkenes and nucleophilic substitution of halogenoalkanes.
items.answer: In addition the electron-rich C=C is attacked by an electrophile and nothing leaves; in substitution a nucleophile attacks a δ+ carbon and a halide leaving group is replaced.
items.markingKey: In addition the electron-rich C=C is attacked by an electrophile and nothing leaves; in substitution a nucleophile attacks a δ+ carbon and a halide leaving group is replaced. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the evidence from enthalpies of hydrogenation that benzene is more stable than a Kekulé structure.
items.answer: Three C=C bonds would release about 3 × −120 = −360 kJ mol⁻¹, but benzene releases only about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, so it is about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than expected.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Three C=C bonds would release about 3 × −120 = −360 kJ mol⁻¹, but benzene releases only about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, so it is about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than expected. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why a two-step route from an alkane to an alcohol via a halogenoalkane gives an impure product.
items.answer: Radical substitution of the alkane gives a mixture of mono- and polysubstituted, and positional isomers of, halogenoalkanes, so the alcohol made from them is also a mixture.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Radical substitution of the alkane gives a mixture of mono- and polysubstituted, and positional isomers of, halogenoalkanes, so the alcohol made from them is also a mixture. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Elena writes: "Bromine reacts with alkenes because Br₂ is a polar molecule." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Br₂ is non-polar; a dipole is induced by the π electrons of the alkene.
items.markingKey: Br₂ is non-polar; a dipole is induced by the π electrons of the alkene. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Lars writes: "Benzene has three double bonds and so reacts like an alkene." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Benzene has a delocalised π system; it does not behave as three isolated C=C bonds and prefers substitution.
items.markingKey: Benzene has a delocalised π system; it does not behave as three isolated C=C bonds and prefers substitution. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between LiAlH₄ and NaBH₄.
items.answer: NaBH₄ is a mild reducing agent that reduces aldehydes and ketones in water or ethanol; LiAlH₄ is stronger, also reduces carboxylic acids, and must be used in dry ether.
items.markingKey: NaBH₄ is a mild reducing agent that reduces aldehydes and ketones in water or ethanol; LiAlH₄ is stronger, also reduces carboxylic acids, and must be used in dry ether. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Calculate the maximum mass of 2-methylbutan-2-ol that can form when 6.60 g of 2-methylbut-2-ene reacts completely with excess steam (with an acid catalyst).
The C–C single bond length is 154 pm and the C=C double bond length is 135 pm. Which statement about the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene is consistent with the delocalised model?
options: All six are equal, at about 140 pm.
Three are 154 pm and three are 135 pm.
items.answer: All six are equal, at about 140 pm.
items.markingKey: B. Intermediate bond order of 1.5.

items.stem: Outline a 2-step synthesis of ethanoic acid from bromoethane. Give the intermediate(s), the reagents and conditions, and the type of each reaction.
items.answer: step 1: bromoethane → ethanol using warm aqueous NaOH (nucleophilic substitution); step 2: ethanol → ethanoic acid using excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heat under reflux (oxidation)
items.markingKey: Step 1: intermediate/product ethanol (1); warm aqueous NaOH (1). Step 2: intermediate/product ethanoic acid (1); excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, heat under reflux (1). Reaction types (1).

items.stem: 1.12 g of 2-methylbut-2-ene reacted with excess steam (with an acid catalyst) and 1.07 g of 2-methylbutan-2-ol was isolated. Calculate the percentage yield.
4.88 g of benzene undergoes chlorination with chlorine with an aluminium chloride (or FeCl₃) halogen carrier. Calculate the mass of chlorobenzene obtained if the yield is 90 %.
A 3-step synthesis has step yields of 72 %, 63 %, 69 %. Calculate the overall percentage yield.
Which alkene from 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, ethene and hex-3-ene gives a mixture of two structural isomers on reaction with HCl?
items.answer: 2-methylbut-2-ene
items.markingKey: D. 2-methylbut-2-ene is unsymmetrical, so Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov products form.

items.stem: ΔH(hydrogenation) values: cyclohexene −121 kJ mol⁻¹, cyclohexa-1,3-diene −230 kJ mol⁻¹, benzene −209 kJ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the stabilisation energy of benzene using cyclohexene as the reference. (b) Estimate it again by treating benzene as cyclohexa-1,3-diene plus one further isolated C=C bond. (c) Evaluate which estimate is more reliable and what both show about the Kekulé model.
items.answer: (a) 3 × (−121) = −363; −209 − (−363) = 154 → 154 kJ mol⁻¹. (b) (−230) + (−121) = −351; −209 − (−351) = 142 → 142 kJ mol⁻¹. (c) The second estimate allows for the small conjugation energy of adjacent C=C bonds, so it is closer to a true “localised triene”; both show that benzene is substantially more stable than any Kekulé structure, so the delocalised model is supported.
items.markingKey: (a) 154 (2). (b) 142 (2). (c) judgement on the reference compound (1); conclusion: Kekulé model inadequate / delocalisation (1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Retrosynthesis is the most effective way to plan an organic synthesis."
items.answer: Retrosynthesis is a powerful planning tool, but each proposed step must be evaluated practically.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: works backwards from the target, revealing simple starting materials; allows comparison of several routes. Arguments against: the reverse reactions may not be practical; yields, cost, safety and selectivity must still be checked. Supported judgement: Retrosynthesis is a powerful planning tool, but each proposed step must be evaluated practically. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem:
A student bubbled excess HBr through a solution containing 4.15 g of 2-methylbut-2-ene at room temperature. 6.79 g of a liquid product mixture was obtained. Gas chromatography showed two peaks:

compound | peak area / %
2-bromo-2-methylbutane | 95
2-bromo-3-methylbutane | 5

(a) Calculate the percentage yield of the product mixture. [3]
(b) Explain the ratio of products in terms of the mechanism. [2]
(c) Calculate the mass of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane in the mixture. [1]
(d) State why the two products have identical molecular formulas. [1]
(e) Suggest why the reaction is carried out in the dark. [1]
items.answer: (a) 76 % (b) 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is major because it forms via the more stable tertiary carbocation; 2-bromo-3-methylbutane forms via a less stable carbocation. (c) 6.45 g (d) They are structural (positional) isomers. (e) To prevent radical substitution side reactions initiated by UV light.
items.markingKey: (a) [3] n(alkene) = 4.15/70.15 = 0.0592 mol (M1); theoretical = 8.94 g (M1); yield = 76 % (A1). (b) [2] carbocation intermediate (1); more alkyl groups / positive inductive effect → more stable (1). (c) [1] 6.79 × 95/100 = 6.45 g (A1), assuming peak area ∝ mass. (d) [1] structural isomers (1). (e) [1] radical reactions avoided (1).

items.stem: "Kekulé's structure of benzene is an adequate model." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It is inadequate: structural and thermochemical evidence supports the delocalised model.

Arguments against: predicts unequal bond lengths – all are 140 pm; predicts addition with bromine water; predicts a hydrogenation enthalpy of −360, not −208 kJ mol⁻¹; predicts two isomers of 1,2-dibromobenzene. Supported judgement: It is inadequate: structural and thermochemical evidence supports the delocalised model.
